title: Unvalidated URL permits arbitrary notification fetches
description: The service accepts an arbitrary URL from its caller and passes it directly to Angular's HTTP client without an allowlist, origin check, or restriction to the intended notification endpoint. If a caller exposes this parameter to attacker-controlled input, an attacker can cause the browser to issue authenticated same-origin GET requests to unintended application endpoints, or make requests to arbitrary external origins. Any response consumed by the caller could then be treated as a system-wide notification despite coming from an untrusted source. The caller is outside this file, so exploitability depends on whether it exposes or derives the URL from untrusted data.

The caller-supplied URL is passed directly to HttpClient.get, causing the browser to issue a request to any selected URL and return its response as a system-wide notification response.

title: Unbounded retrieval of the complete hints collection
description: `getAll()` issues a request for the complete hints collection and provides no pagination, result limit, or other client-side bound. If the backing `/api/Hints/` collection can grow substantially, a caller invoking this method causes the server to serialize and transmit the entire collection and causes the browser to hold the full response in memory. An attacker who can grow the collection, or repeatedly trigger this request, could consume server, network, and client resources. The presence of server-side limits or pagination controls cannot be confirmed from this file.

The method constructs an unparameterized request to the hints collection endpoint and maps the entire returned `response.data` array, with no page size, maximum-result check, timeout, or client-side bound.

title: Unbounded photo upload forwarded to memories endpoint
description: The public `addMemory` method accepts an arbitrary caller-supplied `File` and forwards the complete object in a multipart request without any size or count limit. A caller can repeatedly invoke this method with very large files, consuming client bandwidth and potentially causing the `/rest/memories` upload handler to consume excessive server memory, disk, or processing capacity. Server-side upload limits may exist outside this file, but no such control is visible here and the request is constructed without a bounded payload.

title: Cypress task exposes arbitrary application configuration
description: The Cypress Node task `GetFromConfig` accepts an unrestricted configuration key from its caller and returns the corresponding application configuration value. A test spec or other code able to invoke Cypress tasks can request arbitrary nested configuration entries rather than an allowlisted set, potentially exposing internal endpoints, credentials, or other deployment settings to the Cypress runner and its artifacts. This is limited to the Cypress/test execution boundary rather than a direct production HTTP endpoint, so the impact depends on whether untrusted tests or CI jobs can run.

title: Unbounded retrieval of the entire quantity collection
description: The public `getAll()` method always requests the complete `/api/Quantitys/` collection and provides no page, limit, or cursor controls. The response is then consumed wholesale as `response.data`. If the collection is large or an attacker can repeatedly trigger this operation, each request can consume substantial server bandwidth, server serialization work, and browser memory, potentially degrading availability. The server-side route and any infrastructure limits are outside this file, so the finding is reported with moderate confidence.

title: Configuration endpoint is not constrained to HTTPS
description: The service takes the build-time `environment.hostServer` value verbatim and uses it to construct the configuration endpoint, without enforcing HTTPS or rejecting an insecure scheme. If a deployment sets this value to an HTTP URL, an on-path attacker can read or modify the application configuration response in transit, potentially altering OAuth redirect metadata, feature/security settings, and other client behavior. The file does not establish that the production environment or an interceptor enforces TLS elsewhere, so the finding is conditional on the configured host scheme.

description: The service accepts a caller-supplied wallet private key and transmits it directly to the application server as JSON. A safer ownership-verification workflow would keep the private key client-side and submit a challenge signature or other proof of possession. Exposure through a compromised server, request logging, debugging, or infrastructure handling the request could allow unauthorized control of the wallet.

title: Raw API errors are exposed through browser-console logging
description: The specification explicitly requires API failures to be written directly to the browser console without sanitization, structured context, or redaction. For example, a raw product-search error is propagated through `component.loadProducts()` and the test requires `console.log` to receive the original error value; equivalent expectations exist for order, quantity, delivery-status, price, and quantity-update failures at lines 138-182. If the underlying service returns backend error details, stack traces, identifiers, or other sensitive information, any authenticated user with browser-console access can inspect them, and the application gains no controlled security-audit trail.

The file provides no indication that these values are generated or isolated beyond being test data; this is therefore a low-confidence hardcoded-credential misconfiguration rather than a confirmed production secret exposure.

title: MFA temporary authentication token is exposed to JavaScript via localStorage
description: The MFA temporary authentication token is read from browser `localStorage` and submitted to the verification endpoint. Unlike an HttpOnly, Secure cookie, a localStorage token is accessible to any same-origin JavaScript and persists in browser storage. If an attacker can execute same-origin script, they can steal the pending authentication token and potentially replay or combine it with a captured TOTP code to complete the victim's MFA flow. The token is explicitly used as authentication state (`tmpToken`), so this is an authentication/session-management weakness, although exploitation depends on a separate same-origin script-execution capability and the server's token lifetime/replay controls.

title: Client-side accounting authorization trusts decoded token role
description: The accounting-role decision is made entirely from a decoded client-side token payload. `isAccounting()` calls `LoginGuard.tokenDecode()` and directly trusts `payload.data.role` without any visible signature, issuer, expiration, or server-side authorization check. Because the token is client-readable and the role check is performed in the frontend, a regular user can modify or forge the token payload to set `data.role` to the accounting role, causing the accounting UI gate to return true. The concrete impact visible in this file is bypass of the navbar's accounting privilege gate; if the accounting route relies on this client-side check rather than enforcing the role server-side, unauthorized accounting functionality becomes accessible.

The decoded, client-influenced claim is directly compared with the accounting role and the result is returned as the authorization decision. Altering the token payload can therefore make this check succeed; backend authorization is not established by this client-side decision.

title: Differential security-question lookup enables account enumeration
description: The forgot-password flow exposes an account-enumeration oracle. The test supplies an email address, performs a security-question lookup, and expects a concrete question for a known address but `undefined` for an unknown address. An unauthenticated user who can submit arbitrary email addresses can distinguish registered accounts by observing whether a question is returned or displayed. The lookup endpoint and UI caller are outside this test file, so their exact exposure cannot be confirmed here, but this file explicitly codifies the differential behavior.

title: Caller-controlled basket IDs are used for unscoped basket reads
description: The public `find` method accepts a caller-supplied basket identifier and places it directly in the basket lookup URL. There is no ownership binding or authorization check in this service, and a client-side caller can substitute another user's basket ID or reproduce the request directly. If the corresponding server route does not independently scope the lookup to the authenticated user, this enables BOLA and disclosure of another basket's contents. The same unchecked-ID pattern is also present in `get`, `put`, `del`, `checkout`, and `applyCoupon`.

title: Basket merge fails open after target-basket lookup errors

It attempts to read that basket, but converts every lookup error—including an authorization failure, not-found response, or other server error—into an empty basket and continues. title: Guest basket quantities are trusted without a meaningful upper bound

title: Client-side privileged password policy can be bypassed

The component trusts the mutable `localStorage` value to decide whether the account is privileged, allows passwords as short as five characters, and does not check form validity before submitting. title: OAuth callback does not validate state before selecting the identity
description: The callback accepts an access_token from the ActivatedRoute redirect payload and immediately exchanges it for a profile, but this component performs no OAuth state correlation or validation. An attacker can obtain a valid token for the attacker's own OAuth account, construct or reuse a callback URL containing that token, and induce a victim to visit it. The victim's browser can then be logged into the attacker's account, causing subsequent victim actions or submitted data to be associated with the attacker-controlled identity. This is an OAuth login-CSRF/session-confusion flaw; validation performed inside the service cannot replace a client-side state check tying the response to the victim's initiated authorization request.

There is no check that the requested record belongs to the authenticated user or that the caller has permission to view it. An attacker can request another user's recycle-item identifier and receive that record's data.

The query's where clause forwards that identifier as the sole selection criterion; there is no user identity, ownership predicate, or role-based authorization condition.
When the lookup resolves, the result is forwarded into the promise callback without any authorization or ownership check.
The retrieved record is serialized and returned to the caller, exposing any recycle item matching the supplied identifier.

title: Unauthenticated disclosure of arbitrary users' security questions
description: The security-question endpoint is reachable without authentication and uses the caller-supplied `email` query parameter to select a user's security answer record. It then loads and returns that user's security question. Because there is no authenticated principal or ownership/authorization check, any unauthenticated attacker can submit another user's email and learn that account's security question, exposing an authentication-recovery factor and enabling targeted guessing or account-recovery attacks.

After finding the matching answer record, the handler retrieves the referenced security question and returns it in the response. This is the unauthorized disclosure sink; an attacker can repeat the request with arbitrary users' email addresses.

title: Unsalted MD5 used for authentication data
description: The exported hash helper uses unsalted MD5, which is unsuitable for password storage or other authentication secrets because it is fast and inexpensive to brute-force. If credential paths outside this file use this helper, a database compromise enables efficient offline password cracking.

title: Hardcoded RSA private key enables JWT forgery
description: A fixed RSA private-key literal is embedded in the module and used to sign JWTs. Anyone who obtains the application source or deployed key material can forge tokens containing arbitrary identity and role claims. Those forged tokens are accepted by the public-key JWT middleware, enabling authentication and privilege bypass.

title: Hardcoded HMAC secret permits integrity-token forgery
description: The exported HMAC helper uses a hardcoded secret. Because the key is present in source, an attacker who can inspect the application can generate valid MACs for arbitrary data wherever callers use this helper to protect tokens, request state, or other integrity-sensitive values.

title: Custom role checks accept expired JWTs
description: The custom role middleware verifies only the JWS signature and then decodes the payload. jws.verify does not enforce JWT claims such as exp, and isAccounting proceeds solely on the decoded role. Consequently, a previously valid signed accounting token remains usable after its six-hour expiration when a route relies on this middleware. The same pattern is present in isDeluxe and isCustomer.

An attacker can locally encode a current-month coupon with an arbitrary discount and have the application return that value.

title: Substring-based redirect allowlist enables open redirect

title: Legacy HTML sanitizer can be bypassed for XSS
description: sanitizeLegacy is not an effective HTML sanitizer. title: Public exposure of the incident-support KeePass database
description: The file-serving handler accepts the literal `incident-support.kdbx` as an exception to the public `.md`/`.pdf` allowlist and sends it without any authentication or resource-level authorization check in this handler. title: Poison-null-byte bypass of the public file-type allowlist
description: The handler rejects only `/` as a path separator, but uses platform-dependent `path.resolve`. On Windows, backslashes are path separators, so a request such as `..\\..\\private\\report.pdf` (with backslashes URL-encoded) contains no forward slash, passes the `.pdf` check, and resolves outside `ftp/`. This can disclose matching `.md` or `.pdf` files from parent or absolute Windows paths. The issue is deployment-dependent because POSIX path resolution does not treat backslashes as separators.

title: Continuation codes use hardcoded, forgeable Hashids encoding
description: The continuation values are generated with Hashids using hardcoded, publicly visible salts. Hashids is a deterministic reversible encoding and does not provide a MAC or signature; the 60-character minimum length only changes formatting and does not add entropy or authenticity. Anyone who knows the source-level salt and challenge IDs can reproduce codes for arbitrary ID sets. If the continuation-code consumer treats these values as proof of completed challenges, an attacker can forge a code that claims additional challenges are solved. The consumer is outside this file, but this file issues the unauthenticated, forgeable values.

An attacker can repeatedly invoke these public endpoints; if the challenge table grows substantially, each request can consume database, memory, CPU, and response-encoding resources proportional to the entire matching table, enabling service degradation. The impact is likely low for a small fixed challenge table, but the missing bound is visible in the file.

title: Unauthenticated challenge-notification trigger permits notification spoofing and spam
description: The exported handler is mounted as unauthenticated `GET /rest/repeat-notification`. It accepts a caller-controlled challenge name and invokes `sendNotification` whenever the named challenge is marked solved. The only authorization-like condition is the global `challenge?.solved` check; there is no check that the caller is authenticated, solved the challenge, or is otherwise permitted to trigger the notification. An unauthenticated attacker can therefore repeatedly request any solved challenge name and cause the application's solved-challenge notification behavior, enabling notification spoofing and spam to connected clients.

Because the route has no visible authentication or rate-limit control, repeated requests can spoof or flood challenge notifications and consume notification/backend and client resources.

description: The unauthenticated product-search handler copies the caller-controlled `q` query parameter into a raw SQL string. Although the value is truncated to 200 characters, it is neither parameterized nor safely escaped, so SQL metacharacters can alter the `WHERE` clause. An attacker can submit crafted input such as a quote-based condition to bypass the intended search predicate and potentially extract or manipulate query results, subject to the database driver's statement capabilities.

title: NFT verification accepts any minted wallet address without ownership proof
description: The NFT challenge treats a caller-supplied wallet address as proof that the caller owns or controlled that wallet. title: Unauthenticated progress restoration with forgeable Hashids tokens
description: All three progress-restoration endpoints are unauthenticated and treat a caller-supplied Hashids value as proof that the caller may mark challenges as solved. title: Weak redirect allowlist enables open redirect bypass

An attacker can apply the same bypass to a URL under an attacker-controlled origin, such as `https://evil.example/?x=https://github.com/juice-shop/juice-shop`, causing an open redirect useful for phishing or redirect-based trust abuse.

A reachable client can send a very large or never-ending POST body and exhaust memory or hold test resources, with no application-level body-size limit. The test-only scope reduces impact but does not remove the unsafe network and resource controls.

Repeated characters also produce repeated ciphertexts, leaking structure. This provides no meaningful confidentiality for the announcement and is unsuitable for protecting arbitrary documents; RSA-OAEP should be used to encrypt a random symmetric key, followed by authenticated symmetric encryption for the document.

A failed transfer can therefore burn the faucet's accounting balance and deny future withdrawals, especially when the contract's actual token balance is lower than its independent `balance` value.
